rationale: Mark 9:33-48 runs through the same sequence as Matthew 18:1-9: a dispute over who is greatest, a child set among the disciples, receiving a child "in My name" as receiving Jesus, the millstone, and cutting off hand, foot and eye. One sentence matches closely in this app's BSB: "if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck" occurs in both Matthew 18:6 and Mark 9:42, and "large millstone" and "who believe in Me" occur only in these two verses of the BSB (script searches). In Greek, the SBL, Nestle, Westcott-Hort and Tischendorf texts have mylos onikos, "donkey millstone," in both Gospels, while the Byzantine, Greek Orthodox and Textus Receptus texts of Mark have lithos mylikos (Bible Hub parallel pages). At Mark 9:42 the editions also split on "in Me" (eis eme): the Nestle, Westcott-Hort and Tischendorf texts omit it, the Westcott-Hort/NA27 line brackets it, and the SBL, Byzantine, Greek Orthodox and Textus Receptus texts have it. The same sayings in the same order are why the type is parallel and the label strong, following conn-matt5-salt-mark9 and conn-matt10-fear-luke12. The differences are checkable: Mark sets the scene in a house in Capernaum, where the disciples are silent when asked what they were discussing (Mark 9:33-34); only Matthew has "unless you change and become like little children" (18:3) and "whoever humbles himself like this little child" (18:4); Mark places John's report about the outside exorcist (9:38-41) between the child and the millstone; and Mark's hand-foot-eye sayings end with "their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched" (9:48, a line the BSB sets in quotation marks). Luke 17:1-2 has the stumbling-block woe and the millstone in another setting; a range cannot span books, so it is not part of this row. Which Gospel used which is not graded here.
